all_of: the app publishes its own API specification on a reachable path, typically /openapi.json or /api/openapi.json for FastAPI
at least one operation in that specification carries NO security key while others carry one
that unauthenticated operation returns a field whose value is a credential or a one-time token rather than a public attribute
a gate elsewhere in the app consumes that token: email verification, password reset, invite acceptance or MFA enrolment
any_of: login refuses with a state message such as Inactive user rather than a credential error, naming the gate
the front-end never calls the unauthenticated operation, so it appears nowhere in the bundle and only the specification lists it

chain.action: ask for the published specification before enumerating anything: GET /openapi.json, /api/openapi.json, /swagger.json, /v3/api-docs, /swagger/v1/swagger.json
chain.why: a published specification IS the attack surface, so finding one replaces enumeration entirely. The front-end is a worse source: the entry page here linked only one script, that script contained no fetch call at all, and the API client sat in a second script that only an inner page linked

chain.action: read the security key of every operation, not the path list. Record which operations declare no security while their siblings do
chain.why: an operation with no security is reachable with no credentials. This is one field in a static document and it is the whole bug; extracting the path list and stopping is what turns a ninety-second solve into a forty-minute one

chain.action: follow $ref into components.schemas and read the RESPONSE field names of that unauthenticated operation; look for token, verifyToken, secret, key, hash, otp, code or session
chain.why: an unauthenticated read is only interesting when what it returns is a credential. A name-shaped match is enough to decide whether to send the request

chain.action: create your own account, call the unauthenticated operation with your own identifier, and read your own token out of the response
chain.why: using your own account keeps the probe read-only against other users and needs no guessed email. The token is the gate's own secret, so the gate is now open

chain.action: spend the token on the operation that consumes it, then authenticate normally and read what the gate was protecting
chain.why: the state message on login names the gate before the bypass and stops naming it afterwards, which is the cheapest confirmation that the bypass is what changed

chain.action: before reporting an ownership bug, check whether the protected objects are simply marked public. List them and read the owner and the public flag
chain.why: here every file was owner_id 1 with is_public true, so a verified account reads them all and there is no missing ownership check on the identifier. Reporting an IDOR that is not there is the trap this step exists to close

first_confirming_probe.request: POST /api/userDetails with {"email":"<an account you created>"} and NO Authorization header
first_confirming_probe.expected: 200 with a body containing a credential-shaped field for that account, for example "verifyToken":"<uuid>", proving the operation the specification declared without security really is unauthenticated and really returns a secret
first_confirming_probe.falsifier: 401 or 403, or a 200 whose body carries only public attributes. Then the missing security key is a documentation artefact rather than a bug, and the specification's other unauthenticated operations are the remaining surface

blast_radius: every step is read-only except the account you create yourself. Registration adds one row on a shared instance, which is what the app invites, and verifying that account touches only its own row. Do not call the unauthenticated operation with another player's or a seeded user's identifier and then spend their token: that consumes a one-time secret belonging to someone else and can lock a seeded account out of the intended path for every other player. Read your own and leave theirs alone.

verification.evidence: GET /api/files/5/download on the live instance returned 33 bytes, content-disposition: attachment; filename="flag.txt", whose body was the flag string. Supporting observations from the same run: POST /api/userDetails with no Authorization header returned "verifyToken":"03c8dfa6-97f2-4750-bc7e-68504f2d1fd3"; POST /api/login before verification returned {"detail":"Inactive user"} and after verification returned an access_token; GET /api/openapi.json returned 200 with 8 paths of which only /userDetails, /login, /register and /email-verify lacked a security key.

reuse_when: a target serves its own API specification and at least one operation in it declares no security while siblings do
a response schema in that specification names a field that is a token rather than an attribute
an account state gate stands between registration and use, and login reports that state rather than a credential error
a FastAPI, Flask-RESTX, Spring or ASP.NET app is reachable in a configuration that still publishes its docs route
known_traps: the entry page is not the endpoint inventory. /static/script.js here held no fetch call whatsoever; the API client was in /static/api.js, linked only from an inner page, so recon that follows links from / alone cannot reach it
extracting the path list from the specification and stopping is the expensive mistake. The security key, and the response field names behind $ref, are where the bug is

do not report an ownership bug without checking the public flag. Every file here was owner_id 1 with is_public true, so a verified account legitimately read them all and no check on {file_id} was missing
login answering with a state message such as Inactive user rather than a credential error is the signal that names the gate; a credential error would mean the gate is elsewhere

piping curl with -w into the same file as the body makes the JSON unparseable with Extra data, which reads as a server error rather than a tooling mistake. Write the body with -o and the status with a separate -w

a ten-agent fan-out over this target spent 42 minutes and 1.1M tokens to arrive at the same specification one agent fetched in the first wave. A published specification means the surface is known, so it must END a sweep rather than begin one
an HTB instance expires. The first host answered 200 for roughly fifty minutes and then refused the connection outright, which looks exactly like a blocked probe until you test the port
